passageParagraphs: Memory makes us who we are. It shapes our understanding of the world and helps us to predict what is coming. For more than a century, researchers have worked to understand how memories are formed and then fixed for recall. But those scientists might have been looking at only half the picture. To understand how we remember, we must also understand how, and why, we forget.

Until about ten years ago, most researchers thought that forgetting was a passive process in which memories, unused, decay over time like a photograph left in the sunlight. Then a handful of researchers investigating memory began to bump up against findings that seemed to contradict that decades-old assumption, and they began to put forward the radical idea that the brain is built to forget. A growing body of work suggests that the loss of memories is not a passive process. Rather, forgetting seems to be an active mechanism, constantly at work in the brain; in some animals, the brain's standard state is not to remember, but to forget. A better understanding of this state could lead to breakthroughs in treatments for anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, and even Alzheimer's disease.

Different types of memory are created and stored in varying ways. Autobiographical memories — those of events experienced personally — begin to take lasting form in a part of the brain called the hippocampus in the hours and days that follow the event. Neurons communicate with one another through synapses, and through a process known as synaptic plasticity they constantly produce new proteins to remodel parts of the synapse, selectively strengthening their connections. The more often a memory is recalled, the stronger its neural network becomes. Over time, the memory becomes encoded in both the hippocampus and the cortex, where it is eventually put away for long-term storage. Neuroscientists refer to this physical representation of a memory as an engram.

Much is still unknown about how memories are created, but how the brain forgets has been largely overlooked. It was not at the forefront of Ron Davis's mind when he uncovered evidence of active forgetting in fruit flies in 2012. Davis was studying memory formation in the flies' mushroom bodies — dense networks of neurons that store sensory memories. Intriguingly, he found that dopamine is essential to forgetting. He and his colleagues conditioned flies to associate electric shocks with certain odours, thereby training the insects to avoid them. They then activated the dopaminergic neurons and observed that the flies quickly forgot the association. Yet blocking the same neurons preserved the memory. 'The brain is always trying to forget the information it's already learnt,' Davis says.

A few years later, Oliver Hardt found something similar in rats. Memories are encoded when the strength of the connection between neurons increases, and that connection strength is determined by the amount of a particular type of receptor at the synapse. Known as AMPA receptors, these structures must be maintained for a memory to remain intact. Hardt's lab showed that a dedicated mechanism continuously promotes the expression of AMPA receptors, yet some memories are still forgotten. When he blocked the mechanism behind AMPA-receptor removal in the hippocampus of rats, the animals were prevented from forgetting the locations of objects. Paul Frankland found further evidence that the brain is wired to forget: when new neurons integrate into an adult mouse's hippocampus, the mice forget more. Forgetting, Hardt says, 'is not a failure of memory, but a function of it'.

Researchers think that the human brain might operate in a similar way. Blake Richards suggests that the brain's ability to forget might prevent an effect known as overfit, which occurs when a mathematical model is so good at matching the data it has been trained on that it cannot predict what comes next. In a similar way, if a person remembered every detail of an experience, it might be more difficult to generalize across experiences. 'If you wash out a few details but retain the gist, it helps you to use it in novel situations,' Richards says. 'It's entirely possible that our brain engages in a bit of controlled forgetting in order to prevent us from overfitting to our experiences.'

textWalkthrough.title: The Puzzle and the Radical Idea
textWalkthrough.subtitle: 谜题与激进观点

steps.labelZh: 新观点：大脑为遗忘而生

questions.question: What did most researchers believe about forgetting until about ten years ago?
questions.questionZh: 直到约十年前，多数研究者认为遗忘是怎样的？
questions.answerEn: They believed it was a passive process in which unused memories decay over time, like a photograph left in the sunlight.
questions.answerZh: 他们认为遗忘是被动过程：未被使用的记忆随时间衰退，如同照片在阳光下褪色。

questions.question: How does the opening turn from "how we remember" to "why we forget" — and what device signals the turn?
questions.questionZh: 开头如何从“我们如何记忆”转向“我们为何遗忘”？用什么衔接手段标志这一转折？
questions.answerEn: It opens with the familiar question of how memories form, then turns with "But" to argue that scientists were looking at only half the picture: remembering cannot be understood without forgetting.
questions.answerZh: 先提出熟悉的“记忆如何形成”问题，再用 But 转折指出科学家只看到一半图景：不理解遗忘就无法理解记忆。

questions.question: Why might studying forgetting lead to treatments for anxiety or PTSD?
questions.questionZh: 为什么研究遗忘可能推动焦虑、PTSD 等疾病的治疗？
questions.answerEn: If forgetting is an active, regulated mechanism, then disorders involving intrusive or persistent memories may be cases of faulty forgetting — so understanding the mechanism could point to new treatments.
questions.answerZh: 如果遗忘是主动、可调节的机制，那么与侵入性记忆相关的疾病（焦虑、PTSD）可能是遗忘失灵——理解机制就指向治疗思路。

questions.question: Where do autobiographical memories first take lasting form, and what happens to them over time?
questions.questionZh: 自传体记忆最初在哪里形成持久痕迹？随时间推移它们会怎样？
questions.answerEn: They begin in the hippocampus; through repeated recall they become encoded in both the hippocampus and the cortex, and are eventually stored long-term in the cortex.
questions.answerZh: 它们先在海马体形成；反复提取后同时编码于海马体与皮层，最终长期储存在皮层。

questions.question: What does "plasticity" mean in "synaptic plasticity"?
questions.questionZh: “突触可塑性”中的 plasticity 是什么意思？
questions.answerEn: Plasticity means the ability to change and adapt; synaptic plasticity is the constant remodelling of synapses that lets neurons strengthen or weaken their connections.
questions.answerZh: plasticity 意为“可塑性”：突触可塑性指突触不断重塑，使神经元连接增强或减弱的能力。

questions.question: What pattern is used in "The more often a memory is recalled, the stronger its neural network becomes"?
questions.questionZh: “记忆被提取得越频繁，其神经回路就越强”使用了什么句式？
questions.answerEn: A comparative correlative: "the more…, the stronger…" expresses a proportional relationship — recall frequency directly scales with network strength.
questions.answerZh: 比较关联句式 the more…, the stronger…：表达正比关系——提取越频繁，神经回路越强。

questions.question: What did Davis find about dopamine in fruit flies, and how did he test it?
questions.questionZh: Davis 在果蝇身上发现了多巴胺的什么作用？他是如何验证的？
questions.answerEn: Dopamine is essential to forgetting: activating the dopaminergic neurons made flies quickly forget a shock–odour association, while blocking the same neurons preserved the memory.
questions.answerZh: 多巴胺是遗忘所必需的：激活多巴胺神经元使果蝇迅速忘记“电击—气味”关联；阻断这些神经元则保留记忆。

questions.question: How does the evidence move across paragraphs — and what signals the shift?
questions.questionZh: 证据如何在段落间推进？什么标志了这种转换？
questions.answerEn: It moves from fruit flies (Davis) to rats (Hardt) and mice (Frankland) — a cross-species progression signalled by "A few years later" and parallel block-and-observe experiments.
questions.answerZh: 证据从果蝇（Davis）到大鼠（Hardt）、小鼠（Frankland）逐层推进——由 A few years later 和平行的“阻断—观察”实验标志。

questions.question: Why does Hardt call forgetting "not a failure of memory, but a function of it"?
questions.questionZh: Hardt 为何称遗忘“不是记忆的失败，而是记忆的功能”？
questions.answerEn: Because a dedicated mechanism actively removes AMPA receptors to erase connections; when that removal was blocked, rats stopped forgetting — so forgetting is built-in, regulated work, not decay.
questions.answerZh: 因为存在专门移除 AMPA 受体、清除连接的主动机制；阻断该机制后大鼠不再遗忘——所以遗忘是内置且受调控的功能，而非衰退。

questions.question: What does "overfit" mean, and why does Richards borrow it from artificial intelligence?
questions.questionZh: overfit 是什么意思？Richards 为什么从人工智能领域借用这个词？
questions.answerEn: Overfitting means a model matches its training data so precisely that it cannot predict new data; Richards uses it as an analogy for a memory that keeps every detail and therefore cannot generalise.
questions.answerZh: 过度拟合指模型对训练数据拟合得过于精确，以致无法预测新数据；Richards 借它类比“记住一切细节、无法泛化”的记忆。

questions.question: According to Richards, how does forgetting help us use past experience in new situations?
questions.questionZh: 按 Richards 的观点，遗忘如何帮助我们把过往经验用于新情境？
questions.answerEn: By washing out a few details while retaining the gist, we avoid being trapped by specific instances and can apply the essence of an experience elsewhere.
questions.answerZh: 忘掉部分细节、保留要旨，我们才不会被具体实例困住，能把经验的要点迁移到新情境。

questions.question: Do you think a perfect memory would be a blessing or a burden? Give reasons.
questions.questionZh: 你认为完美的记忆是福还是祸？请说明理由。
questions.answerEn: Open response — strong answers weigh the trade-off: rich recall can help, but remembering every detail may make it harder to extract the gist and can feed obsessive thinking.
questions.answerZh: 开放性回答——有力回答会权衡得失：丰富的回忆有帮助，但记住一切细节可能让人难以提取要旨，并助长强迫倾向。

deepDive.title: Four Threads Through the New Science of Forgetting
deepDive.subtitle: 遗忘新科学的四条线索
deepDive.question: What four ideas weave through the article's account of the new science of forgetting?
bulletsEn: Forgetting was long treated as passive decay; researchers now argue the brain is actively built to forget.
Dopamine in flies, AMPA-receptor removal in rats and neurogenesis in mice all point to active forgetting.
Memories exist as changing synaptic connections; forgetting works by dismantling or rewriting them.
Controlled forgetting prevents 'overfitting', supports generalisation, and may guide treatments for anxiety, PTSD and Alzheimer's.
deepDive.summaryEn: The article describes a paradigm shift: forgetting is not memory failure but an adaptive brain function, backed by evidence across species and promising for treatment.
bulletsZh: 遗忘长期被视为被动衰退；研究者如今认为大脑天生就是要遗忘的。
果蝇的多巴胺、大鼠的 AMPA 受体移除、小鼠的神经发生，都指向主动遗忘。
记忆以不断变化的突触连接存在；遗忘通过拆除或改写连接实现。
受控遗忘防止“过度拟合”、支持泛化，并可能为焦虑、PTSD 与阿尔茨海默病提供治疗思路。
deepDive.summaryZh: 文章描述了一场范式转变：遗忘不是记忆的失败，而是大脑的适应功能，有跨物种证据支持，并蕴含治疗前景。

trueFalse.text: Until recently, most scientists believed that forgetting was an active process.
trueFalse.reason: The article says most researchers thought forgetting was a passive process in which unused memories decay over time.

trueFalse.text: In Davis's experiments, blocking dopaminergic neurons preserved the flies' memory of the shock–odour association.
trueFalse.reason: Activating the neurons made the flies forget quickly, while blocking the same neurons preserved the memory.

trueFalse.text: Hardt found that actively removing AMPA receptors at synapses strengthens long-term memory.
trueFalse.reason: It is the maintenance of AMPA receptors that keeps a memory intact; their active removal is what allows forgetting.

trueFalse.text: Increasing neurogenesis in adult mice made them forget more.
trueFalse.reason: Frankland's 2014 study found the opposite of better memory: more new neurons meant the mice forgot more.

trueFalse.text: Richards believes that remembering every detail helps people generalise across experiences.
trueFalse.reason: He argues that controlled forgetting — washing out details while keeping the gist — prevents overfitting and supports generalisation.
